questions.q: Rolling stock means:
options: The train itself — its coaches, systems and everything the operator interfaces with
Only the track vehicles in the depot
questions.explain: Rolling stock is the train; the 'interface' is everything the operator touches or depends on in it.

questions.q: TCMS stands for:
questions.explain: Train Control and Management System (TCMS) is the train's computer network, giving health and fault data to the crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: The role of Train Control and Management System (TCMS) is to:
options: Provide the train's health and fault data to the crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Most modern train faults are first 'seen' through Train Control and Management System (TCMS) by Operations Control Centre (OCC), not by looking at the train.

questions.q: Which of these is a train system the operations team interfaces with?
questions.explain: Operations interfaces with traction/braking, doors, HVAC, lighting, Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS), Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and fire detection on the train.

questions.q: Regenerative braking means:
options: Brakes are regenerated daily in the depot
While braking, the traction motors act as generators and feed electrical energy back to the Overhead Equipment (OHE)
Energy is wasted as heat only
It works only on diesel trains
questions.explain: Regeneration returns braking energy to the supply system instead of wasting it as heat.

questions.q: Key operational data received from the train includes:
options: Fault alarms, brake status, door status, speed and location
questions.explain: Fault alarms, brake/door status, speed and location flow from the train to crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: In modern trains, most faults are first detected:
options: By Operations Control Centre (OCC)/Train Control and Management System (TCMS) alarms, not by physically looking at the train
By station staff watching the platform
questions.explain: The train reports itself — Operations Control Centre (OCC) usually sees the fault data before anyone sees the train.

questions.q: The traction interlock ensures that:
options: The train cannot take power (traction) while a passenger door is detected open
questions.explain: Like a lift refusing to move with open doors, a doubt about doors means no movement — fail-safe.

questions.q: The emergency brake system on a train is designed to be:
options: Operated only by Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Disabled when Automatic Train Operation (ATO) is on
Fail-safe — loss of air/electrical continuity applies the brakes
questions.explain: If the brake continuity is lost, brakes apply automatically — the failure itself creates the safe state.

questions.q: A deadman's vigilance device protects against:
options: Driver incapacitation — it stops the train if the driver stops responding
questions.explain: The operator must acknowledge at intervals; no response means emergency braking.

questions.q: How does the deadman's device know the driver has stopped responding?
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) watches the cab camera continuously
The driver must acknowledge/actuate it at intervals; silence triggers emergency brake application
questions.explain: Periodic acknowledgement proves vigilance; a missed cycle applies the emergency brake.

questions.q: A defective passenger door on a coach should be dealt with by:
options: Removing the coach immediately at any cost
Isolating that door as per procedure and continuing under control
Asking passengers to hold it shut
Cancelling the train in all cases
questions.explain: Door isolation is the standard controlled response — the faulty door is taken out of service, not fought with.

questions.q: Fire detection in coaches is part of which interface?
options: The train's on-board safety systems interfacing with crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) power control
questions.explain: Coach fire detection alerts crew/Operations Control Centre (OCC) so the emergency response can start early.

questions.q: The train operator's cab-to-Operations Control Centre (OCC) radio is:
options: Part of the rolling-stock operating interface
questions.explain: The cab radio links the operator to Operations Control Centre (OCC) — it is part of how the train is operated, not an extra.

questions.q: The train cab is best compared to:
options: A car's dashboard — displays and warnings that tell the operator the machine's state
questions.explain: Speed, door lights and fault warnings in the cab play the same role as a car's dashboard, at railway scale.

questions.q: A warning indication in the cab that a coach has a fault should lead the operator to:
options: Follow the procedure for that fault, e.g. isolate the affected coach/equipment and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Ignore it until the terminus in all cases
Stop and evacuate immediately for every alarm
Switch off Train Control and Management System (TCMS)
questions.explain: Alarms have defined procedures — isolate where prescribed, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), and continue or withdraw as the procedure says.

questions.q: Namo Bharat trainsets are built by:
options: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), at Delhi
questions.explain: Namo Bharat trainsets are Alstom-built at Savli, aerodynamic and designed for Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) speeds.

questions.q: Namo Bharat trainsets are normally formed of:
questions.explain: The extract describes 6-coach (expandable) aerodynamic trainsets.

questions.q: The design speed of Namo Bharat trainsets is:
questions.explain: Design speed 180 kmph; operational maximum is 160 and average about 100 — do not mix them.

questions.q: Which train system keeps passengers comfortable and is an operations interface?
questions.explain: HVAC, lighting and Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) inside the train are all systems the operations team interfaces with.

questions.q: Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) inside the train helps operations by:
options: Letting crew/Operations Control Centre (OCC) see passenger-area situations without being physically present
questions.explain: On-board Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) feeds situational awareness to crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC) during incidents.

questions.q: If Train Control and Management System (TCMS) shows a brake status fault on one coach before departure, the correct approach is:
options: Depart anyway since one coach does not matter
Cancel all services on the line
Ask passengers to check the brakes
Follow the prescribed fault procedure and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) before deciding to run
questions.explain: Brake status is safety data — the procedure and Operations Control Centre (OCC) decide, not guesswork.

questions.q: A door status indication shows 'open' even after the close command at a station. The train:
options: Cannot take traction power because of the door interlock, until the door is proved closed or isolated
Opens all Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) permanently
questions.explain: The traction-door interlock blocks movement on a door doubt — check, close or isolate the door first.

questions.q: Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) inside the train is used by operations to:
options: Announce stops, destinations and safety/disruption information to passengers
questions.explain: On-board Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) keeps passengers informed, which is an operational duty during disruptions.

questions.q: Why does Operations Control Centre (OCC) need train location and speed data continuously?
options: To regulate the service, protect separation and respond to incidents
questions.explain: Location and speed are core operational data for supervision, regulation and emergency response.

questions.q: The interface between the operator and the train mainly consists of:
options: Cab controls, door controls, brakes, TMS screens and alarms
questions.explain: Cab controls, door controls, brakes, TMS displays and alarms are what the operator actually works with.

questions.q: If the train's fire detection raises an alarm in a coach, the first information path is:
options: Passengers inform the station by phone
It appears in the next day's report
Alarm to the crew (and Operations Control Centre (OCC) via train systems) so the fire procedure can begin
questions.explain: On-board detection alerts the crew/Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately — early warning is its whole purpose.

questions.q: Which statement about regenerative braking is correct?
options: It is used only at depots
It feeds energy back to the Overhead Equipment (OHE)/supply system while slowing the train
questions.explain: During regenerative braking the motors generate, returning energy to the overhead supply.

questions.q: A train reports repeated door faults from the same coach during service. The operationally sound decision is typically:
options: Keep resetting it indefinitely without informing anyone
Open all doors manually at every station
Isolate the defective door/coach function as per procedure, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), and withdraw or attend the train as directed
Ignore it because doors are not safety items
questions.explain: Repeated faults are handled by isolation, Operations Control Centre (OCC) information and a planned withdrawal/attention — not endless resets.

questions.q: The operator notices an unusual cab alarm he cannot identify. Best action?
options: Silence it and continue without telling anyone
Treat it as a real fault: follow the alarm procedure and contact Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Wait for the next day's maintenance report
questions.explain: Unidentified alarms are treated seriously — procedure plus Operations Control Centre (OCC) communication is the interface working as designed.

questions.q: The pantograph on the train roof interfaces with the Overhead Equipment (OHE) to:
options: Collect electric current for traction while keeping safe, continuous contact at speed
questions.explain: The pantograph presses against the contact wire of the Overhead Equipment (OHE) with controlled pressure — too little causes arcing and power loss, too much damages the wire.

questions.q: Sanders fitted on a train are used to:
options: Drop sand on the rail head to improve wheel–rail grip when starting or braking on slippery rails
questions.explain: Sand increases adhesion on wet or leaf-contaminated rails, helping the train accelerate and brake without slipping or sliding.

questions.q: Wheel Slide Protection (WSP) during braking works by:
options: Detecting an axle that is sliding and momentarily easing its brake so the wheel keeps rotating
questions.explain: A sliding wheel grinds a flat spot on itself and stops braking well; Wheel Slide Protection (WSP) releases and reapplies that axle's brake rapidly to keep it turning.

questions.q: The train's battery system is an operations interface because, if the main power supply fails, it:
options: Drives the train to the next station by itself
Keeps emergency lighting, controls and communication alive for a limited time
questions.explain: Batteries are the train's built-in backup — like an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS), they keep the most essential systems alive long enough to detrain passengers safely.

questions.q: If a train fails in a section and cannot move at all, it can be rescued by another train mainly because trains are fitted with:
options: Couplers that let a healthy train attach and push or pull the failed train to a station or depot
Spare engines in the last coach
questions.explain: Compatible couplers and brake connections let a rescue train move a dead train clear of the running line — the standard way to reopen a blocked section.
